metaDescription: Corded electric dethatchers compared by motor amps, working path, bag size and depth settings, so you can pick one that clears thatch without stalling.
expertTake: The WEN DT1516 leads this guide on the strength of 15 amp motor to 3300 RPM. For the lowest entry cost the SENIX 15-inch is the sensible route, with the caveat of less proven brand. Skip corded machines if the lawn is far from an outlet or full of obstacles that snag a cable. A cordless model is easier there.
introParagraphs: A corded dethatcher never runs out of battery, which is the whole case for it. The price of that freedom is a cable, and the rest of the decision is about motor strength, reel design and how much thatch a bag can hold before you stop.
This guide ranks corded 2-in-1 machines by motor rating, working path and depth control, and it explains why cord gauge matters as much as amperage when the grass is thick.

buyingCriteria.explanation: Bag capacity decides how often you stop. The Sun Joe AJ808E carries 13.2 gallons and the MZK 15-inch carries 12, and thick thatch fills any bag fast. Plan on emptying a bag several times on a quarter acre. Look for a zipper or latch that you can operate with the machine running.

Working width runs from 14 inches on the Greenworks 13A 14-inch to 16 inches on the WEN DT1516. A wider path means fewer passes, but it needs a stronger motor and a larger bag, and it is harder to steer around beds and trees. Under about a quarter acre, the narrower models are often the better handlers. Measure gate clearance, since the machine body can be wider than the path.

Tine and blade material decide durability. Stainless or spring steel resists rust better than plain carbon steel, and bent tines should be replaced rather than reused. The Westinghouse 16-inch and the Sun Joe AJ808E both use replaceable tines, so a spare set is cheap insurance. Dull or bent parts tear grass instead of lifting thatch.

Power source shapes the whole ownership. Corded models like the WEN DT1516 run indefinitely but need a heavy-gauge outdoor cord, ideally 14 gauge or thicker, to avoid voltage drop. Cordless machines trade the cord for runtime, so match battery capacity to lawn size. Every pick in this set is corded, which avoids runtime anxiety.

Corded motors are rated in amps and cordless ones in volts and battery capacity. The WEN DT1516 lists 15 amp, up to 3300 RPM. Higher amperage holds rpm in dense thatch, but a 15 amp tool is already at the limit of a 15 amp household circuit, so it must not share the outlet with anything else. Compare rpm only between machines with the same reel type.

Dethatch when the grass is actively growing and recovering. Early fall is best for cool-season lawns and late spring for warm-season grass, with soil moist but not soaked. Mow short first, make the first pass at the shallowest depth, then rake and overseed. Even a capable machine like the WEN DT1516 will damage a dormant or drought-stressed lawn.

faq.q: How do I know if I need to dethatch?
faq.a: Cut a small plug and measure the spongy brown layer between grass and soil. If it is thicker than about half an inch, dethatching helps; thinner than that, leave it. A machine like the Westinghouse 16-inch is overkill for a thin layer.

Some listings, such as the Sun Joe AJ808E, are labeled dethatcher and aerator, but the blade reel only slices thin grooves in the surface. It does not remove soil cores. For true compaction relief, use a core aerator separately.

faq.q: How long an extension cord can I use?
faq.a: Use a heavy-gauge outdoor cord, 14 gauge or thicker for long runs, and keep it as short as practical. A thin cord drops voltage and makes the motor stall. Plug the machine into a circuit that is not shared with other heavy loads.

faq.q: Is a cordless dethatcher strong enough?
faq.a: For small to mid-size lawns, yes, if you have enough battery capacity. Heavy thatch drains packs quickly, so plan on a spare. Corded models such as the WEN DT1516 have no runtime limit.

faq.q: When is the best time to dethatch?
faq.a: Dethatch when the grass is actively growing, early fall for cool-season grass and late spring for warm-season grass. Soil should be moist but not soaked. Avoid dethatching during drought or dormancy.

faq.q: Can I dethatch a wet lawn?
faq.a: Avoid it. Wet soil clumps, bogs the reel and tears roots. Wait until the surface is dry but the soil is still slightly moist, and work in two perpendicular passes at the shallowest depth first.
